name: Complete TQL Statement Syntax
title: Complete TQL Statement Syntax
text:
Complete TQL Statement Syntax
 
 
  
  

  
   The syntax of a complete SELECT TQL statement is as follows:

   SELECT [ DISTINCT ] { * | { expression [ [ AS ] alias ] [ , ... ] } }
  FROM table_reference [ [ AS ] alias ] [ , ... ]
  [ { join_type JOIN table_reference ON condition } [ , ... ] ]
  [ WHERE condition_expression ]
  [ GROUP BY { expression } [ , ... ] [ HAVING condition ] ]
  [ ORDER BY { expression } [ ASC | DESC ] [ , ... ] ]
  [ [ START start ] LIMIT limit ]
  [ UNION [ ALL ] select_query ]
   
     
    
     
      In the preceding syntax, uppercase words are TQL keywords. In actual TQL statement writing, these keywords can be either uppercase or lowercase. However, a keyword cannot contain both uppercase and lowercase letters.

      The square brackets indicate that the content in the brackets is not mandatory.

      You can select only one of the contents separated by the pipe character (|).

      The contents in curly brackets ({}) are complete and you need to avoid sentence breaking errors.

      [, ...] indicates that the content in front of [, ...] can be repeated for multiple times.

     

    

   

   

   
    
    SELECT Clause

    A SELECT clause is used to describe the content to be provided in the query result. The SELECT clause syntax is as follows:

    SELECT [ DISTINCT ] { * | { expression [ [ AS ] alias ] [ , ... ] } }
    
     DISTINCT
      If the DISTINCT keyword is specified, only one record is retained in the query result, that is, duplicate records are deleted. Note that duplication is for an entire record not for a single field.

     *
      An asterisk (*) indicates that if no GROUP BY clause is used in the TQL statement, all fields in the model or subquery (for details about subquery, see FROM Clause) specified by the FROM clause are queried. Otherwise, all grouping result fields are queried.

     expression
      The results of the expression specified by expression in the clause are returned in the query results. The results can consist of property names, functions, operators, and other expressions. For details, see Operators and Expressions. The expression is subject to the GROUP BY... HAVING clause. For details, see GROUP BY... HAVING Clause.

     AS
      AS indicates the keyword that separates the expression and alias, and can be omitted.

     alias
      alias indicates the alias of the expression in the clause. The field name in the query result set indicates the alias. Its format is the same as that of an identifier.

    

    Example:

    To query the title and author from the book model, run the following statement:

    select title, author from book
    To query unique categories and authors from the book model, run the following statement:

    select distinct category, author from book
   

   
    
    FROM Clause

    The FROM clause is used to describe the source of the data to be queried. The data source can be model data or data of other subqueries. The FROM clause syntax is as follows:

    FROM table_reference [ [ AS ] alias ] [ , ... ]
   

   
     
    
     When the FROM clause is used to query multiple models at the same time, use the FROM and JOIN model names (aliases must be used if aliases are defined for the model names) in clauses that use model properties, such as the SELECT and WHERE clauses, to limit the model to which the properties belong to avoid ambiguity.

    

   

   
    table_reference
     The table_reference syntax is as follows:

     model_reference | { ( select_query ) }

    AS
     AS indicates the keyword that separates the expression and alias, and can be omitted.

    alias
     alias indicates the alias of table_reference in the clause, which facilitates reference in the JOIN... ON and WHERE clauses. Its format is the same as that of an identifier.

    model_reference
     model_reference indicates that a model can be referenced. The value of model_reference can be a model name or model URI. For example, a model name indicates the model in the same project as the asset to which the current TQL statement belongs to. However, whether a model name can be used depends on the application scenario of the TQL statement. If you use a model URI, enclose the model URI in double quotation marks ("") because the URI contains the special characters slashes (/).

    select_query
     You can use another complete SELECT TQL statement, which is the subquery statement of the FROM clause.

   

   Example:

   To query the book's title and category, and the author's name and nationality, run the following statement:

   select b.title, b.category, a.name, a.nationality from book as b, author as a where b.author_id = author.id
   For details about other examples, see SELECT Clause and JOIN... ON Clause.

   
    
    JOIN... ON Clause

    A JOIN ... ON clause is used to describe the association of multiple data sources. This clause can be used to associate models or other subqueries. The JOIN ... ON clause syntax is as follows:

    { [ join_type ] JOIN table_reference [ [ AS ] alias ] ON condition_expression } [ , ... ]
    
      
     
      
       The JOIN... ON clause is optional and does not need to be written if other models or subqueries do not need to be associated.

       When using the JOIN ... ON clause to connect multiple models, use the FROM and JOIN model names (aliases must be used if aliases are defined for the model names) in clauses that use model properties, such as the SELECT, JOIN ... ON, and WHERE clauses, to limit the model to which the properties belong to avoid ambiguity.

      

     

    

    
     join_type
      join_type indicates the connection type. This parameter is optional. If it is not written, the default value INNER is used. The values are as follows:

      
       INNER: inner connection. The intersection of the left and right tables is used.

       LEFT: left connection. The whole left table is used. The records that do not exist in the right table are replaced with null.

       RIGHT: right connection. Use the whole right table. The records that do not exist in the left table are replaced with null.

       FULL: full connection. The union set of the left and right tables is used. The records that do not exist in the other table are replaced with null.

      

      
        
       
        For JOIN statements in the MySQL database, join_type cannot be set to FULL.

       

      

     table_reference
      table_reference indicates the data source of the right table. It is the same as table_reference in the FROM clause.

     AS
      AS indicates the keyword that separates the expression and alias, and can be omitted.

     alias
      alias indicates the alias of table_reference in the clause, which facilitates reference in the JOIN... ON and WHERE clauses. Its format is the same as that of an identifier.

    

    
     condition_expression
      condition_expression indicates expression of the connection relationship between tables on the left and right sides of JOIN. The value must be a Boolean expression. For details, see Operators and Expressions. Note that this parameter can be used only to describe the relationship between associated tables and cannot be used to filter data in a single table. The expression for filtering data in a single table should be written in the WHERE clause.

    

    Example:

    To query the book's title and category, and the author's name and nationality, run the following statement:

    select b.title, b.category, a.name, a.nationality from book as b join author as a on b.author_id = author.id
   

   
    WHERE Clause

    A WHERE clause is used to filter data in the data source specified by the FROM clause. Only the data that meets the conditions specified by the WHERE clause can be queried and then be processed by other clauses. The WHERE clause syntax is as follows:

    WHERE condition_expression
   

   
     
    
     
      The WHERE clause is optional. If it is not specified, all data in the data source specified by the FROM clause is valid.

     

    

   

   
    condition_expression
     condition_expression indicates the expression used to filter the data specified by the FROM and JOIN... ON clauses. The value must be a Boolean expression. For details, see Operators and Expressions.

   

   Example:

   To query the names of English scientific books, run the following statement:

   select b.title from book where category = 'science' and language = 'English'
   
    
    GROUP BY... HAVING Clause

    A GROUP BY... HAVING clause is used to group the original data that meets the conditions of the WHERE clause and filter the grouping results. The GROUP BY... HAVING clause syntax is as follows:

    GROUP BY { expression } [ , ... ] [ HAVING condition_expression ]
   

   
     
    
     
      The GROUP BY... HAVING clause is optional. If it is not written, the original data is not grouped.

      If the GROUP BY clause is used, the SELECT and ORDER BY clauses cannot be used to directly query the original data. Only the following content can be used:
       
        Expression in the GROUP BY clause

        Aggregation operation performed on the original query results

       

     

    

   

   
    expression
     expression indicates the expression for calculating the original data. The calculation results obtained using the expression are grouped. The results can consist of property names, functions, operators, and other expressions. For details, see Operators and Expressions.

    condition_expression
     condition_expression indicates the expression for filtering the grouping results. The value must be a Boolean expression. For details, see Operators and Expressions. Note that only the expressions in the GROUP BY clause can be used to perform aggregation operations on the original grouping results. The original grouping data cannot be directly used.

   

   Example:

   To count the number of books in each category, run the following statement:

   select category, count(1) as count from book group by category
   To query categories with more than 100 books, run the following statement:

   select category, count(1) as count from book group by category having count(1) > 100
   
    ORDER BY Clause

    An ORDER BY clause is used to sort query results. The ORDER BY clause syntax is as follows:

    ORDER BY { expression } [ ASC | DESC ] [ , ... ]
    
      
     
      
       The ORDER BY clause is optional. If it is not written, the results are returned in the original order.

       If the results are returned in the original order (that is, the order is not specified), the order in which the results are returned each time after the same query is performed may be different.

       When you sort fields with duplicate data, the order of these duplicate records may be different after each sorting.

      

     

    

    
     expression
      expression indicates the expression used to sort the calculation results. The results can consist of property names, functions, operators, and other expressions. For details, see Operators and Expressions. The expression is subject to the GROUP BY... HAVING clause. For details, see GROUP BY... HAVING Clause.

     ASC and DESC
      ASC or DESC indicates that the system sorts data records in ascending or descending order, respectively. If these parameters are not specified, the system sorts data records in ascending order.

    

    Example:

    To sort the book titles in ascending order, run the following statement:

    select title from book order by title
    To sort author names and nationalities in ascending order, run the following statement:

    select name, nationality from author order by name, nationality
   

   
    START... LIMIT Clause

    A START ... LIMIT clause is used to limit the specified part of the result set to be returned by the current query. This clause is commonly used for returning a large-size result set whose data needs to be displayed on different pages. The START ... LIMIT clause syntax is as follows:

    [ START start ] LIMIT limit
    
      
     
      
       The START ... LIMIT clause is optional. If it is not specified, all results are returned. However, this clause is limited by other specifications.

       START start is optional. If it is not set, the default value 0 is used.

       When the START ... LIMIT clause is used for returning results on different pages, to ensure that data on each page is not repeated and lost, the START ... LIMIT clause must be used with the ORDER BY clause, and data must be sorted by unique fields.

      

     

    

    
     start
      start indicates the sequence number from which the query result is returned. The sequence starts from 0.

     limit
      Maximum number of query results that can be returned. The actual number of returned results depends on the value of limit and the actual number of data records. For example, if limit is set to 1000 and the actual number of data records is 500, only 500 data records are returned. If the actual number of data records is 2000, 1000 data records are returned.

      If the value of limit is not restricted, 1000 is used by default. That is, a maximum of 1000 data records can be returned by default.

      In the statement, the maximum value of limit defined by developers is 5000. That is, a maximum of 5000 data records can be returned.

    

    Example:

    To sort the book titles in ascending order, display 10 data records on each page, and return the results from page 5, run the following statement:

    select title from book order by title start 40 limit 10
   

   
    UNION Clause

    A UNION clause is used to combine multiple query result sets and obtain the union set. The UNION clause syntax is as follows:

    UNION [ ALL ] select_query
   

   
     
    
     
      The UNION clause is optional, and does not need to be specified if you do not need to concatenate other query result sets.

      If you are sure that the combined result sets do not contain duplicate records, (for example, the values of some fields must be different in each result set), add the ALL keyword to avoid extra performance overhead caused by removing duplicate results.

      The START... LIMIT clause can be used in both query statements connected by the UNION clause. Each START... LIMIT clause takes effect on the query results of the statements that are connected by the UNION clause. The START ... LIMIT clause that appears at the end of the statement takes effect for the last SELECT query, not for the results obtained using the entire UNION clause.

      When using the UNION clause, you must specify the START... LIMIT clause for each query to avoid an excessively large-size result set.

      The union set of data returned by the UNION clause must comply with the constraints for limit. If limit is not specified or the specified value is greater than 1000, a maximum of 1000 data records can be returned.

     

    

   

   
    ALL
     If the ALL keyword is specified, all data of the two result sets is retained. Otherwise, duplicate records are removed.

    select_query
     You can write another complete SELECT TQL statement.

   

   Example:

   To query the names of all teachers and students (a maximum of 100 teachers and 100 students), run the following statement:

   (select name, 'teacher' as role from teacher order by id limit 100) union (select name, 'student' as role from student order by id limit 100)
   

  

  
   
    
     Parent topic: TQL Statements Used for Model Data Query

name: Data Filtering TQL Statement Syntax
title: Data Filtering TQL Statement Syntax
text:
Data Filtering TQL Statement Syntax
 
 
  
  

  
   As a subset of the complete TQL statements, the data filtering TQL statements support only the data filtering of a single model, that is, only the WHERE clause (without the WHERE keyword), ORDER BY clause, and START... LIMIT clause are supported. The syntax of a complete data filtering TQL statement is as follows:

   condition_expression
  [ ORDER BY { expression } [ ASC | DESC ] [ , ... ] ]
  [ [ START start ] LIMIT limit ]
   For details about the syntax, see the description of the corresponding clause in Data Filtering TQL Statement Syntax.

   
     
    
     
      Whether the ORDER BY and START... LIMIT clauses are supported depends on the application scenarios.

     

    

   

   
    Example:
    
     To query English scientific books and sort them by title in ascending order, run the following statement:
      category = 'science' and language = 'English' order by title

     To query the person whose name is Tom and age is older than 20 and the person whose name is Jim and age is older than 30, run the following statements:
      name = 'Tom'
(name = 'Tom' and age > 20) or (name = 'Jim' and age > 30)

    

   

   This type of TQL statements can be used to query a single data record and query lists in service orchestration.

  

  
   
    
     Parent topic: TQL Statements Used for Model Data Query

name: Introduction to the Elastic Model TQL Statements
title: Introduction to the Elastic Model TQL Statements
text:
Introduction to the Elastic Model TQL Statements
 
 
  
  

  
   TQL statement query capabilities supported by elastic models are a subset of statements described in Complete TQL Statement Syntax and Data Filtering TQL Statement Syntax. However, the elastic model TQL statements also have some unique functions. The differences are as follows:

   
    The elastic model does not support associated query. That is, the JOIN ... ON and UNION clauses, and the FROM clause that contains multiple models are not supported.

    The elastic model does not support subqueries. That is, subqueries cannot be used in the FROM clause, and operators, such as in, that support subqueries do not support subqueries.

    Elastic models and common data models support different TQL functions. For details, see TQL Functions.

    Elastic models and common data models support different expression operators and operands. For details, see Operators and Expressions.

   

  

  
   
    
     Parent topic: TQL Statements Used for Model Data Query

parent.name: TQL Statements Used for Model Data Query

name: Operators and Expressions
title: Operators and Expressions
text:
Operators and Expressions
 
 
  
  

  
   Expressions (described as expression and condition_expression in the preceding topics) can be used in clauses, such as SELECT and WHERE, to describe a calculation. The calculation result can be a numeric value, string, or Boolean value (true or false). In the preceding topics, expressions described as condition_expression refer to those whose calculation results are Boolean values. An expression consists of operands and operators.

   
    Operands

    For TQL statements used for model data query, the operand can be one of the following. The specific operand that can be used depends on its location.

    
     
      
       Table 1 Operands
      
      
       
       
      
      
       
        
         Operand Type

        
         Description

       

      
      
       
        
         Model property

        
         A model property is presented in the form of identifiers. The model property format should meet the identifier format conditions. For details, see Identifier.

         In the scenario where multiple models are associated for query and subqueries exist, to prevent ambiguity of multiple properties with the same name in the same context, add a model name (or alias of the model name in the query) in front of the property name and the alias of the subquery to distinguish these properties.

       

       
        
         Constant

        
         A constant can be a digit, string, or Boolean value.

       

       
        
         Function

        
         For details, see TQL Functions.

       

       
        
         Expression

        
         For details, see Expression.

       

      
     
    

    

   

   
    Operator

    An operator can be one of the following. The specific operator that can be used depends on its location.

    
     
      
       Table 2 Operators and expressions
      
      
       
       
       
      
      
       
        
         Operator and Expression

        
         Description

        
         Example

       

      
      
       
        
         Logical operator

        
         Connects two logical expressions based on the specified logical relationship to form a larger logical expression.

        
         -

       

       
        
         a AND b

        
         Connects a and b based on the AND relationship.

        
         If a is true and b is false:

         The result of a AND b is false.

       

       
        
         a OR b

        
         Connects a and b based on the OR relationship.

        
         If a is true and b is false:

         The result of a OR b is true.

       

       
        
         Test operator

        
         Determines whether a condition is met, and forms a logical expression with an operand.

        
         -

       

       
        
         a = b

         a IS b

         a != b

         a IS NOT b

        
         Determine whether a is equal to b. These expressions can be used to determine numeric values and character strings, but the types of a and b must be the same.

         IS and IS NOT are operators compatible with ADC1.0. Their meanings are the same as = and (!=). Assets developed in ADC 2.0 should use operators = and !=.

        
         If a is equal to b:

         The result of a = b is true.

         The result of a IS b is true.

         The result of a != b is false.

         The result of a IS NOT b is false.

       

       
        
         a > b

         a >= b

         a < b

         a <= b

        
         Compare a and b. These expressions can be used to compare numeric values and character strings, but the types of a and b must be the same.

         
           NOTE: 
          
           The elastic model does not support comparison of character string sizes.

          

         

        
         If a is 1 and b is 2:

         The result of a > b is false.

         The result of a >= b is false.

         The result of a < b is true.

         The result of a <= b is true.

       

       
        
         a [ NOT ] IN ( b [ , ... ] )

        
         Determines whether a is in a list formed by operands such as b. These expressions can be used to determine numeric values and character strings, but the types of operands, such as a and b, must be the same.

        
         name in ('Tom', 'Jim', 'John'): indicates that the condition is met when name is Tom, Jim, or John.

         age not in (25, 26, 27): indicates that the condition is met when age is not 25, 26, or 27.

       

       
        
         a [NOT] IN (select_query)

        
         Determines whether a is in the query result of select_query. select_query is a complete TQL statement. For details, see Complete TQL Statement Syntax. The query results obtained using select_query must be returned, and only one column of data is returned.

         
           NOTE: 
          
           The elastic model does not support this operator.

          

         

        
         title in (select title from book where category = 'science')

       

       
        
         a IS [NOT] NULL

        
         Checks whether a is null.

        
         name is null: indicates that the condition is met when name is null.

         name is not null: indicates that the condition is met when name is not null.

       

       
        
         a IS [NOT] EMPTY

        
         Checks whether a is empty.

         In any of the following scenarios, a is empty:

         
          null

          Null character string

          Null object

          Empty array

          If a is a variable, no value is transferred for the variable.

         

        
         name is empty: indicates that the condition is met when name is empty.

         name is not empty: indicates that the condition is met when name is not empty.

       

       
        
         a BETWEEN b AND c

        
         Determines whether a is within the range of [b,c]. The value of b must be less than or equal to the value of c. This expression is equivalent to a >= b AND a <= c. This expression can be used to compare numeric values and character strings, but the types of a, b, and c must be the same.

         
           NOTE: 
          
           The elastic model does not support comparison of character string sizes.

          

         

        
         age between 25 and 30: indicates that the condition is met when age is within the range of [25,30].

       

       
        
         a [ NOT ] LIKE b [ IGNORE CASE ]

        
         Checks whether a matches b. Wildcards are supported. IGNORE CASE indicates that the value is case-insensitive. If it is not specified, the value is case-sensitive. Only character strings can be checked.

         The following wildcards can be used for b:

         
          %: indicates that any number of characters (including 0) can be matched.

          _: indicates that any character can be matched.

         

         
           NOTE: 
          
           The elastic model does not support case-insensitive values.

          

         

        
         name like ' %o %': indicates that the condition is met when name contains o. The value of name is case-sensitive. For example, Tom and John meet the condition, but O'Brien does not meet the condition because the case condition is not met.

       

       
        
         a [ NOT ] CONTAINS b [ IGNORE CASE ]

        
         Checks whether a matches b. Wildcards are not supported. IGNORE CASE indicates that the value is case-insensitive. If it is not specified, the value is case-sensitive. Only character strings can be checked.

         
           NOTE: 
          
           The elastic model does not support case-insensitive values.

          

         

        
         name contains'o': indicates that the condition is met when name contains o. The value of name is case-sensitive. For example, Tom and John meet the condition, but O'Brien does not meet the condition because the case condition is not met.

       

       
        
         a [ NOT ] STARTS b

        
         Checks whether the value of a starts with b. The value of a is case-sensitive. Only character strings can be checked.

        
         name starts 'J': indicates that the condition is met when name starts with the letter "J". For example, Jim and John meet the condition.

       

       
        
         a [ NOT ] ENDS b

        
         Checks whether the value of a ends with b. The value of a is case-sensitive. Only character strings can be checked.

        
         name ends 'm': indicates that the condition is met when name ends with the letter "m". For example, Tom and Jim meet the condition.

       

       
        
         [ NOT ] EXISTS ( select_query )

        
         Determines whether the query using select_query contains data. select_query is a complete TQL statement. For details, see Complete TQL Statement Syntax.

         Note that for performance purposes, you should use select_query to specify that only one data record can be returned and that only a column of data needs to be returned.

        
         exists (select title from book where category = 'science' limit 1): indicates that the condition is met when a book whose category is science exists.

       

       
        
         Arithmetic operator

        
         Performs numeric calculation. The result is generally a numeric value.

        
         -

       

       
        
         a + b

         a - b

         a * b

         a / b

         a % b

        
         Perform addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and remainder operations on a and b. Only numeric values can be calculated.

        
         -

       

      
     
    

    
      
     
      
       Operators are case-insensitive. In the preceding table, operators are in uppercase and operands are in lowercase to distinguish operators from operands.

       Although in the TQL syntax, identifiers can be used as operands on the left and right of a test operator, identifiers should be used as operands on the left and constants should be used as the operand on the right due to the limited TQL capability in the model data query scenario.

      

     

    

   

   
    
    Expression

    According to the content returned by the expression, the expressions can be classified into the following types:

    
     Logical expression: generally consists of test operators, logical operators, and corresponding operands. The expression returns a Boolean value. Logical expressions can also be connected by logical operators to form a larger logical expression, for example:
      name starts with 'Tom'
name starts with 'Tom' or name starts with 'Jim'

     Arithmetic expression: generally consists of arithmetic operators and corresponding operands. The expression returns a numeric value, for example:
      3.14 * r * r

    

    To specify the priority of expression calculation, you can use parentheses ().

   

  

  
   
    
     Parent topic: TQL Statements Used for Model Data Query

text:
TQL Functions
 
 
  
  

  
   This section describes the usage of TQL functions.

   
     
    
     TQL functions are supported by default in data models and elastic models.

     In external data source models, TQL functions marked as Supported can be used only after a tenant administrator configures a tenant-level parameter whitelist. Configuration menu path: Products and Services > Administration > System Settings in the runtime-state environment

     
      Name: Set it to ext_datasource_tql_func_allowlist.

      Category: Set it to model.

      Encrypt: Disable it.

      Value: Set it to the function name without brackets. Multiple function names are separated with commas (,). For example, CURRENT_DATE,CURRENT_TIME.

     

    

   

   
    
     
      Table 1 TQL functions
     
     
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
     
     
      
       
        Name and Syntax

       
        Description

       
        Application Scenario

       
        Example

      

      
       
        Data Model

       
        Elastic Model

       
        External Data Source Model

       
        Vector Model

      

     
     
      
       
        Date and Time Functions

      

      
       
        CURRENT_DATE()

       
        This function returns the current date. The time is UTC time in yyyy-MM-dd format.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        current_date()

      

      
       
        CURRENT_TIME()

       
        This function returns the current time. The time is UTC time in HH:mm:ss format.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        current_time()

      

      
       
        NOW()

       
        This function returns the current date. The time is UTC time in yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        Supported

        This function can only be used in a SELECT clause.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        now()

      

      
       
        DATE_ADD(time, interval)

       
        If the value of interval is a positive integer, the time obtained by adding the interval specified by interval to the time specified by time is returned.

        If the value of interval is a negative integer, the time obtained by subtracting the interval specified by interval from the time specified by time is returned.

        The time is in yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format. This function is irrelevant to the time zone.

        Parameter:

        
         time: time in yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format

         interval: time interval. For details, see Time Interval Expressions.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        date_add('2021-01-02 12:34:56', '1H')

        Return: 2021-01-02 13:34:56

        

        date_add('2021-01-02 12:34:56', '-1H')

        Return: 2021-01-02 11:34:56

      

      
       
        DATE_SUB(time, interval)

       
        The usage is opposite to that of DATE_ADD.

        If the value of interval is a positive integer, the time obtained by subtracting the interval specified by interval from the time specified by time is returned.

        If the value of interval is a negative integer, the time obtained by adding the interval specified by interval to the time specified by time is returned.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        date_sub('2021-01-02 12:34:56', '1H')

        Return: 2021-01-02 11:34:56

        

        date_sub('2021-01-02 12:34:56', '-1H')

        Return: 2021-01-02 13:34:56

      

      
       
        DATE_FORMAT(time, format)

       
        Returns the format of the date or time specified by time.

        Parameter:

        
         time: time in yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format

         format: time format. The supported formats are listed in Date and Time Formats.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        date_format('2021-01-02 12:34:56', 'yyyy/MM/dd HH:mm')

        Return: 2021-01-02 12:34

      

      
       
        YEAR(time)

       
        Returns the year of the specified date or time. This function is irrelevant to the time zone.

        Parameter:

        
         time: time in yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        year('2021-01-02 12:34:56')

        Return: 2021

      

      
       
        MONTH(time)

       
        Returns the month of the specified date or time date. This function is irrelevant to the time zone.

        Parameter:

        
         time: time in yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        month('2021-01-02 12:34:56')

        Return: 1

      

      
       
        TO_SECONDS(time)

       
        Returns the number of seconds between the specified date or time date and 0000-00-00 00:00. There is no legal date, and the value can be the same as that of MySQL. This function is irrelevant to the time zone.

        Parameter:

        
         time: time in yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        to_seconds('2021-01-01')

        Return: 63776678400

        to_seconds('2021-01-01 00:00:01')

        Return: 63776678401

      

      
       
        TO_DAYS(time)

       
        Returns the number of days between the specified date or time date and 0000-00-00 00:00. There is no legal date, and the value can be the same as that of MySQL. This function is irrelevant to the time zone.

        Parameter:

        
         time: time in yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        to_days('2021-01-01')

        Return: 738156

        to_days('2021-01-01 00:00:01')

        Return: 738156

      

      
       
        TO_DATE(time, format)

       
        Returns a value that is the same as that of DATE_FORMAT.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

      

      
       
        DATE(time)

       
        Returns the date part of a specified date or time date. This function is irrelevant to the time zone.

        Parameter:

        
         time: time in yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss format

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        date('2021-01-01')

        Return: 2021-01-01

        date('2021-01-01 00:00:01')

        Return: 2021-01-01

      

      
       
        CURRENT_TZ()

        

       
        Parameter: none.

        This function indicates the time zone of the current user. If it is unavailable, use the time zone of the current tenant. This function works with CONVERT_TZ().

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        Input: CURRENT_TZ()

        Response example: PRC

      

      
       
        CURRENT_USER()

       
        Parameter: none.

        This function indicates the current user account.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        CURRENT_USER()

        Response example: admin

      

      
       
        DATEDIFF()

       
        Parameters:

        
         d1: date

         d2: date

        

        This function subtracts two dates (d1 and d2).

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        The DATEDIFF(d1,d2) function subtracts two dates (d1 and d2).

        DATEDIFF('2016-08-16 18:00:00','2016-08-15 09:00:30')

        Return: 1

      

      
       
        day_of_month(time)

        

       
        Parameter: time (time)

        The value of time indicates the day number in the current month and ranges from 0 to 31.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        DAY_OF_MONTH (d) returns the day number of the current month.

        DAY_OF_MONTH ('2016-08-06 08:00:00')

        Return: 6

      

      
       
        day(time)

       
        Parameter: time (time)

        This function returns the date value in time.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        day(time) returns the date value in time.

        day('2016-08-06 08:00:00')

      

      
       
        day_of_week(time)

       
        Parameter: time (time)

        time indicates the day number of a week. The number 1 indicates Sunday and the number 2 indicates Monday.

        This function returns a day of week specified by time. The returned numbers comply with ISO8601 standards. Numbers 1 to 7 indicate Monday to Sunday.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The DAY_OF_WEEK (d) function returns the day number of a week.

        DAY_OF_WEEK('2016-08-06 08:00:00')

        Return: 7

      

      
       
        day_of_year(time)

       
        Parameter: d (date)

        d indicates the day number of the current year and ranges from 1 to 366.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        DAY_OF_YEAR (d) returns the day number of the current year.

        DAY_OF_YEAR('2016-08-06 08:00:00')

        Return: 219

      

      
       
        hour(time)

       
        Parameter: t (time)

        This function extracts the hour in a time expression (t).

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        The HOUR(t) function extracts the hour in a time expression (t).

        HOUR('2016-08-06 08:00:00')

        Return: 8

      

      
       
        MICROSECOND()

       
        Parameter: dt (date and time)

        This function returns the microseconds from the time or date expression. The value ranges from 0 to 999999.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        The MICROSECOND(dt) function returns the microseconds from the time or date expression. The value ranges from 0 to 999999.

        microsecond('2008-09-10 07:15:30.123456')

      

      
       
        MINUTE()

       
        Parameter: t (time)

        This function returns the minute in a time expression (t).

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The MINUTE(t) function returns the minute in a time expression (t).

        MINUTE('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

        

      

      
       
        MONTH()

       
        Parameter: d (date)

        This function returns the month from the date (d) passed.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        The MONTH(d) function returns the month from the date (d) passed.

        MONTH('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

      

      
       
        QUARTER()

       
        Parameter: d (date)

        This function returns the quarter from the date (d) passed.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The QUARTER(d) function returns the quarter from the date (d) passed.

        QUARTER('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

      

      
       
        SECOND()

       
        Parameter: t (time)

        This function returns the second in a time expression (t).

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        The SECOND(t) function returns the second in a time expression (t).

        SECOND('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

      

      
       
        SUBTIME()

       
        Parameters:

        
         t: time

         n: second

        

        This function subtracts n seconds from the time given by t.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The SUBTIME(t, n) function subtracts n seconds from the time given by t.

        SUBTIME('2018-04-12 08:06:04','59')

      

      
       
        TIME()

       
        Parameter: dt (date and time)

        This function returns the time or the time of a datetime expression.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The TIME(dt) function returns the time or the time of a datetime expression.

        TIME('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

      

      
       
        TIMEDIFF()

       
        Parameters:

        
         t1: time

         t2: time

        

        This function returns the difference between two time points, (t1-t2).

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The TIMEDIFF(t1,t2) function returns the difference between two time points, (t1-t2).

        TIMEDIFF('2016-08-16 08:00:00','2016-08-1509:00:30')

      

      
       
        TIMESTAMP()

       
        Parameters:

        
         d: date

         diff: date offset

        

        The TIMESTAMP(d) function returns the date expression. The TIMESTAMP (d, diff) returns d+diff.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        TIMESTAMP(d) / TIMESTAMP(d,diff),

        
         TIMESTAMP(d): returns a date expression.

         TIMESTAMP (d,diff): returns d+diff

        

        timestamp('2018-03-12 05:00:00','03:00:02')

        timestamp('2018-03-12 05:00:00')

      

      
       
        TO_LOCAL_TIME()

       
        Parameter: utctime

        This function converts the UTC time to the local time using the time zone of the current tenant.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The TO_LOCAL_TIME(utctime) function converts the UTC time to the local time using the time zone of the current tenant.

        to_local_time('2018-03-02 12:12:23')

      

      
       
        WEEK()

       
        Parameter: d (date)

        This function returns the calendar week of the date, which ranges from 1 to 53.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The WEEK(d) function returns the week number, which ranges from 1 to 53.

        WEEK('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

      

      
       
        WEEKDAY()

       
        Parameter: d (date)

        his function returns the day number of a week. 0 indicates Monday and 1 indicates Tuesday.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The WEEKDAY(d) function returns the day number of a week. 0 indicates Monday and 1 indicates Tuesday.

        WEEKDAY('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

      

      
       
        week_of_year()

       
        Parameter: d (date)

        This function returns the calendar week of the date, which ranges from 1 to 53.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The WEEK_OF_YEAR(d) function returns the calendar week of the date, which ranges from 1 to 53. WEEK_OF_YEAR ('2018-04-12 08:06:04')

      

      
       
        YEARWEEK()

       
        Parameters:

        
         date: date

         mode: start flag of a week

        

        This function returns the year and week.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        The YEARWEEK(date[,mode]) function returns the year and week. The value of mode can be 0 to 7. The details are as follows:

        
         0: Sunday, 0-53.

         1: Monday, 0-53.

         2: Sunday, 1-53.

         3: Monday, 1-53.

         4: Sunday, 0-53.

         5: Monday, 0-53.

         6: Sunday, 1-53.

         7: Monday, 1-53.
          YEARWEEK('2018-04-12 08:06:04',1)

        

      

      
       
        time_floor(time,period)

       
        Parameters:

        
         time: time, which is in this format: yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss [DST].

         period: time granularity

        

        This function rounds the time down according to the period to an adjacent period.

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        The TIME_FLOOR(time, period) function rounds the time down according to the period to an adjacent period.

        The time granularity is defined as follows:

        
         2s: 2 seconds

         1m: 1 minute

         5m: 5 minutes

         15m: 15 minutes

         1H: 1 hour

         2H: 2 hours

         12H: 12 hours

         1d: 1 day

         1W: 1 week

         1M: 1 month

         1Q: 1 quarter

         1Y: 1 year
          time_floor(now(), '1W')

        

      

      
       
        Numeric Calculation Functions

      

      
       
        ROUND(number [, decimals])

       
        Returns the value of number truncated by the number of decimal places. The truncated part is rounded off. If the last digit of the decimal part is 0, the digit is not retained.

        Parameters:

        
         number: Enter a number or an expression that returns a number.

         decimals: number of decimal places to be reserved. The default value is 0. If the value is a negative number, the corresponding integer position is replaced with 0.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        round(123.451, 2)

        Return: 123.45

        round(123.456, 0)

        Return: 123

        round(123.456, -2)

        Return: 100

        round(1.101, 2)

        Return: 1.1

      

      
       
        FLOOR(number)

       
        Returns an integer that is less than or equal to the nearest number.

        Parameter:

        
         number: Enter a number or an expression that returns a number.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        floor(123.456)

        Return: 123

        floor(-123.456)

        Return: -124

      

      
       
        CEIL(number)

       
        Returns an integer that is greater than or equal to the nearest number.

        Parameter:

        
         number: Enter a number or an expression that returns a number.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        ceil(123.456)

        Return: 124

        ceil(-123.456)

        Return: -123

      

      
       
        ABS(number)

       
        Returns the absolute value of number.

        Parameter:

        
         number: Enter a number or an expression that returns a number.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        abs(123.456)

        Return: 123.456

        abs(-123.456)

        Return: 123.456

      

      
       
        GREATEST()

       
        Parameter: a group of values to be compared

        This function returns the maximum one among the values.

        If the argument contains null, null is returned. Otherwise, the maximum value is returned.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        Input: greatest(5,6,7,8,9)

        Return: 9

      

      
       
        LEAST()

       
        Parameter: a group of values to be compared

        This function returns the smaller value when two or more arguments are available.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        Input: least(5,6,7,8,9)

        Return: 5

      

      
       
        MOD()

       
        Parameters:

        
         N: dividend

         M: divisor

        

        This function returns the remainder of N divided by M.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        Input: mod(9,5)

        Return: 4

      

      
       
        POWER()

       
        Parameters:

        
         X: base number

         Y: exponent

        

        This function returns the value of X raised to the power of Y.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        Input: power(2,3)

        Return: 8

      

      
       
        SQRT()

       
        Parameter: X: number

        This function returns the square root of the number specified by X.

       
        MySQL

       
        -

       
        -

       
        MySQL

       
        Input: sqrt(16)

        Return: 4

      

      
       
        Character Processing Functions

      

      
       
        CONCAT(string [ , ... ])

       
        Returns a string obtained by concatenating multiple strings of the input parameter.

        Parameter:

        
         string: string to be combined. You can enter multiple strings.

        

        
          NOTE: 
         
          When CONCAT contains the ROUND function, if the last digit of the decimal part returned by the ROUND function is 0, the GaussDB discards the last digit, but the MySQL database retains it. When the CONCAT function is used for combination, the system cannot intervene, leading to differences.

          For example, the returned results of concat(round(10/2, 1), ' %') are 5% and 5.0%, respectively, for GaussDB and MySQL databases.

         

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        concat('Hello', ' ', 'world', '!')

        Return: Hello world!

      

      
       
        LENGTH(string)

       
        Returns the number of bytes of the returned input parameter. Counts the number of bytes of characters in UTF-8 encoding.

        Parameter:

        
         string: character string to be processed.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        length('Hello')

        Return: 5

      

      
       
        CHAR_LENGTH(string)

       
        Returns the number of characters of the input parameter.

        Parameter:

        
         string: character string to be processed.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        char_length('Hello')

        Return: 5

      

      
       
        LOWER(string)

       
        Returns the character string converted to lowercase letters.

        Parameter:

        
         string: string to be converted.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        lower('Hello')

        Return: hello

      

      
       
        UPPER(string)

       
        Returns a converted uppercase character string.

        Parameter:

        
         string: string to be converted.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        upper('Hello')

        Return: HELLO

      

      
       
        SUBSTRING(string, start [, length])

       
        Returns the string length starting from the start position.

        Parameters:

        
         str: string to be truncated.

         start: start position of the truncation. The value of this field starts from 1. A negative number means that the truncation starts from right to left.

         length: length of the truncated string. This parameter is optional. If it is left blank, all characters from the start position are truncated.

        

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

       
        -

       
        GaussDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL

       
        GaussDB, MySQL

        Null Value Processing Functions

      

      
       
        IFMISSING($var, action [, value])

        IFNULL($var, action [value])

        IFEMPTY($var, action [, value])

        IFEMPTYSTR($var, action [, value])

       
        When the value of the $var variable is null, the action specified by action is performed. Otherwise, the value of the $var variable is returned.

        The conditions for the four functions to determine whether the value of the $var variable is empty are different:

        IFMISSING: If the value of $var is missing (not transferred through an input parameter), the condition is met.

        IFNULL: The condition is met when the value of $var is null.

        IFEMPTY: The condition is met when the value of $var is missing (not transferred through the input parameter), null, an empty character, an empty object, or an empty array.

        IFEMPTYSTR: If the value of $var is an empty string, the condition is met.

        Parameters:

        
         var: variable name.

         action: (Note that the value of this parameter is a string constant and must be enclosed in single quotation marks, indicating that different processing actions when the value of $var meets the condition.) The value options are as follows:
          
           'ignore': Ignores the minimum test operator expression of the current function.

           'value': The value specified by the value parameter is returned.

          

         value: indicates the value returned by the current function when the value of the $var variable meets the condition and the value of the action parameter is 'value'.

        

       
        Database-independent

        The null value processing function can only be used to check whether the input parameter is null. (Not transferred, null, empty string, empty object, empty array) When the input parameter meets the corresponding condition, the specified value is returned. The value cannot be used to process model data.

        

       
        title = $title and author = ifmissing($author, 'ignore')

        If the value of the $author variable is not transferred, the expression of the test operator of the ifmissing function does not take effect. The preceding expression is equivalent to title = $title.

        Otherwise, the above expression is equivalent to: title = $title and author = $author

        

        title = $title and author = ifempty($author, 'value', 'Unknown')

        If the value of the $author variable is not transferred, null, an empty object, or an empty array, the preceding expression is equivalent to title = $title and author = 'Unknown'.

        Otherwise, the above expression is equivalent to: title = $title and author = $author

    Time Interval Expressions

    The time interval is usually used to indicate information such as the difference between two times and periods. The DATE_ADD and DATE_SUB functions support the specified interval. The time interval is expressed in these TQL statements as a string consisting of an integer and a unit of time. The values of the time unit are as follows:

    
     s: Second

     m: Minute

     H: Hour

     D: Day

     W: Week

     M: Month

     Q: Quarter

     Y: Year

    

    Example:

    
     1m: 1 minute

name: FAQs
title: FAQs
text:
FAQs
 
 
  
  

  
   
    In the TQL Statement with GROUP BY Clauses, the SELECT Clause Queries the Original Property and the Property Is Not in the Aggregate Function

    For example, the following statement is incorrect:

    select title, category from book group by category
    The preceding statement is used to perform grouping based on category. However, the original title property is queried using the SELECT clause. A category may contain different titles. Therefore, it is inappropriate to use any title as the title of the category. Therefore, this query is invalid. Even if this query can be performed, the results are uncertain.

    
     If the GROUP BY clause is used, the SELECT and ORDER BY clauses cannot be used to directly query the original data. Only the following content can be used:
     
      Expression in the GROUP BY clause

      Aggregation operation performed on the original query results

     

    

   

   
    Sorting of NULL Values in RDB

    
     MySQL does not support specifying nulls first/last and considers that the NULL value is the smallest. Therefore, when processing TQL queries, MySQL ignores the sorting policy of NULL values specified by users.

     GaussDB supports specifying nulls first/last. The NULL values entered by users can be used for sorting.

name: TEL Overview
title: TEL Overview
text:
TEL Overview
 
 
  
  

  
   Top Expression Language (TEL) is a unified expression calculation language of ADC. It can be roughly seemed as expressions in SQL statements, but the syntax and capabilities are different. The functions and capabilities of TEL vary according to application scenarios. However, when the same semantics are to be expressed, the writing of TEL statements is the same.

  

  
   
    Basic Concepts of TEL Statements

    Differences Between TQL and TEL Statements

   

   
    
     Parent topic: TEL Syntax Reference

name: Basic Concepts of TEL Statements
title: Basic Concepts of TEL Statements
text:
Basic Concepts of TEL Statements
 
 
  
  

  
   
    
    Identifier

    An identifier is used to refer to a specific object that is determined by the specific scenario and its position in the TEL statement.

    Identifiers are case sensitive. In most cases, an identifier must start with a letter followed by letters, digits, and underscores (_). If special characters such as spaces are required in an identifier, enclose the special characters with double quotation marks (""). For details, see Quotation Mark.

    An identifier can be separated by dots (.), which is commonly used in the scenario where a field in a table is referenced by a table name or alias. A maximum of two dots can be used in an identifier, that is, the identifier is divided into three parts. When a dot (.) is used to separate identifiers, if double quotation marks ("") are required, write the dot (.) outside the double quotation marks(""), for example, "book"."author".

   

   
    Constant

    A Constant refers to a fixed value, character string, and specific values (such as null).

    Numeric constants include decimal integers and decimals, for example, 100 and 3.14.

    A string constant must start and end with a single quotation mark ('). The content quoted in the single quotation mark is a character string. For details, see Quotation Mark.

   

   
    Function

    A function encapsulates the data processing logic to implement specific functions. After a function is executed, the corresponding result is returned. Available functions vary depending on the application scenarios. Functions with the same name may have different semantics and usage in different scenarios.

   

   
    Operator and Operand

    When writing TEL expressions, use operators to process operands. Operators can be used to process one or more operands and can be placed before, after, or between operands. After the processing is complete, the processing result is returned. Operands can be identifiers, constants, variables, functions, and other expressions. The operators and operands that can be used vary depending on scenarios.

   

   
    Expression

    Consisting of operators and operands, an expression is a formula that expresses the logical meaning of one or more data processing operations. Expressions can be combined using operators to form more complex processing logic expressions.

   

   
    
    Quotation Mark

    Different quotation marks in TEL statements have different meanings. The following quotation marks can be used in TEL statements:

    
     Double quotation marks (" "): are used to indicate identifiers. For details, see Identifier. If double quotation marks ("") and backslashes (\) need to be used in an identifier, add a backslash (\) in front of the double quotation marks ("") and backslashes (\) for escape, For example, "username" indicates the identifier username. This identifier does not need to be escaped because it does not contain quotation marks ("). "identifier with \"double quote\"" indicates the identifier identifier with "double quote". You need to use backslashes (\) to escape the double quotation marks (") in TQL statements because this identifier contains double quotation marks (").

     Single quotation marks ('): are used to indicate a string constant. For details, see Identifier. If single quotation marks (') need to be used in a character string, add a backslash (\) in front of the single quotation marks (') for escape. For example, 'ADC' and '123' indicate the ADC and 123 character strings, respectively. These character strings do not need to be escaped because they do not contain single quotation marks ('). 'You\'re welcome.' indicates the character string You're welcome. You need to use a backslash (\) to escape the single quotation mark (') in TQL statements because this character string contains a single quotation mark (').

    

   

  

  
   
    
     Parent topic: TEL Overview

name: Differences Between TQL and TEL Statements
title: Differences Between TQL and TEL Statements
text:
Differences Between TQL and TEL Statements
 
 
  
  

  
   The main functions and application scenarios of TQL and TEL statements are different. In a specific scenario, only either of them is used. For details, see the development guide for the specific scenario. For example, TQL statements instead of TEL statements are used for model data query.

   
    TQL statements are used for query.
     TQL statements are used to query data that meets the specified conditions from the existing data based on the criteria specified in TQL statements. A typical scenario is as follows: During model data query, TQL statements are used to specify query conditions and further calculate the query result (such as grouping and aggregation).

    TEL statements are used for the expression calculation.
     TEL statements are used to calculate the given data based on the expressions specified in TEL statements to obtain the calculation result.

   

   Other differences are as follows:

   
    Variables can be used in TQL statements but cannot be used in TEL statements.
     TQL statements are used in the scenario where a trigger is triggered by a business logic (for example, the business side calls a service or an API of a model). You can use a variable as a placeholder in a TQL statement, and the calling party transfers a specific value to obtain a complete TQL statement for execution.

     However, TEL statements are generally used when data is changed (for example, the model data is changed). Therefore, a parameter (that is, an identifier in a TEL statement) calculated by a TEL statement comes from the context of the TEL statements (for example, model data that is actually changed). Additional values don not need to and cannot be transferred through mechanisms, such as variables.

   

   TQL statement examples in the model data query scenario:

   author = 'Tom' -- Data filtering TQL statement, which is used to query the data whose author is Tom
select title from book where author = 'Tom' and nationality = $nationality -- Complete TQL statement, which is used to query the book whose author is Tom and the author's nationality is transferred by a variable
select author, count(1) as count from book group by author -- Complete TQL statement, which is used to collect statistics on the number of works of each author
   

  

  
   
    
     Parent topic: TEL Overview

SQL Editing Description
 
 
  
  

  
   In service configuration of ADC develop state, ADC uses DataService Query under Platform Services to provide the SQL editor for the Yacht service to edit SQL statements for accessing Data Cube data in Yacht mode.

   However, SQL statements in the develop state can only be edited. Statements cannot be directly compiled, executed, and debugged. To compile and execute statements, go to the runtime-state page.

text:
Identifiers
 
 
  
  

  
   
    Description

    
     The standard syntax SQL3 (SQL99) is used.

     The MySQL syntax set is used.

     Currently, only SELECT statements of DML are supported. Only some DDL statements are supported.

     The columns, tables, and functions in SQL statements will be strictly verified.

         Single-line comment

        
         A line containing double minus signs (-), a space, and content.

        
         -- hello

       

       
        
         Multi-line comment

        
         Text starts with /* and ends with */.

        
         /*

         Simple identifier

        
         A simple identifier consists of ASCII characters, including letters from A to Z that is case insensitive, digits from 0 to 9, and underscores (_).

         
           NOTE: 
          
           
            The matching of simple line identifiers is case insensitive.

            The escape character of the identifier is the back quote (`).

            Using the escape character is not recommended because the escape character may cause incompatibility in cross-database scenarios.

            The identifier can start with a digit only when it contains an escape character.

            The identifier can contain a maximum of 64 characters.

           

          

         

        
         select ABC from TABLE;select ABC123 from TABLE;select `abc123` from TABLE;

       

       
        
         Attribute identifier

        
         [Schema name.]Table name.Column name

         
           NOTE: 
          
           If a column name conflict occurs, the table name and schema name must be carried to specify column.

         All columns

        
         * indicates all columns.

         [Schema name.]Table name.* indicates all columns in the table.

         
           NOTE: 
          
           * is converted to the actual column for execution. If * contains columns with the same name, an error occurs.

          

         

        
         SELECT * FROM t1;
SELECT t1.*, s1.t1.* FROM t1;

         Second in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)

        
         The special character string starting with TIMESTAMP indicates the UTC in second.

         (TIMESTAMP 'YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss.xxx')

         
           NOTE: 
          
           When the special character string starting with TIMESTAMP is used, write it in brackets [()].

          

         

         
           CAUTION: 
          
           
            Time starting with TIMESTAMP is not supported in ClickHouse.

            Time starting with TIMESTAMP cannot be used for query in the SQL statement editing pane of Module.

           

          

         

        
         select (TIMESTAMP '2020-02-22 22:22:22.222');

        
         java.sql.Timestamp

        
         TIMESTAMP

       

       
        
         Interval

        
         INTERVAL

         
           CAUTION: 
          
           
            Time type starting with INTERVAL is not supported because the intervals of data engines differ greatly and cannot be unified.

            The time needs to be converted to the numeric type for calculation.

           

          

         

        
         -

        
         -

        
         -

       

       
        
         Boolean

        
         TRUE: The corresponding value is 1.

         FALSE: The corresponding value is 0.

         
           CAUTION: 
          
           TRUE and FALSE are not supported in ClickHouse.

          

         

        
         select TRUE, FALSE;

        
         boolean

        
         BOOLEAN

       

       
        
         Null

        
         NULL indicates that there is no data and is used as a placeholder.

         
           CAUTION: 
          
           NULL is not supported by ClickHouse.

          

         

        
         select NULL;

        
         null

        
         -
